answer:
I ran the experiment twice on emerald:mock, which is IQM's simulator of the emerald chip. I did not use the real emerald. The real chip is out of budget for this request, as you said. Mock jobs cost 0 credits.

What I ran: I asked the API for the real emerald's current list of couplers. It lists 54 qubits and 85 CZ couplers. I built the kicked Ising model directly in the chip's own gates. The model has 3 steps. Each step turns all 54 qubits by RX(theta) and then applies one RZZ(-pi/2) on each of the 85 couplers. Each RZZ(-pi/2) becomes exactly one CZ gate plus a Z turn that the chip does for free by shifting phases. The 4 circuits use theta = 0, 0.2 pi, 0.35 pi and 0.5 pi, at 250 shots each, in one job. I skipped every compiler step, so nothing could add, merge or remove gates. I read the circuits back from the server. Each circuit has 255 CZ gates (85 couplers times 3 steps) and 162 PRX gates, and each measures QB1 to QB54. The test job was 01a16489-5770-7490-820e-24c5fcc55a4f. The final job was 01a16489-a2f2-7127-b54c-7f93ed3b7b24. The API reports billed_seconds = 1.0 for the final job. Both are in job_log.txt in the worktree.

Ideal magnetization (exact simulation of the submitted circuits, with no noise): 1.000 at theta 0, 0.452 at 0.2 pi, 0.113 at 0.35 pi, and 0.000 at 0.5 pi. This shows the effect you asked about. A stronger sideways field tips the spins more, so the sheet loses more of its magnetization. At 0.5 pi it is gone.

Measured magnetization on the mock: -0.016, 0.022, 0.005 and -0.018. All four values are close to 0, and they do not follow theta. The mock returns random bitstrings that do not depend on the circuit, so these numbers carry no physics. The noise-corrected values divide each value by the theta = 0 value of -0.016. They come out to rescaled_02 = -1.35, rescaled_035 = -0.33 and rescaled_05 = 1.12. These numbers are meaningless, because they divide noise by noise. On the real chip, the theta = 0 value would land somewhere below 1 because of errors. That correction would then make sense.

Could an ordinary laptop compute this? Yes, and it did. After 3 steps, each qubit's result depends only on qubits at most 2 couplers away. That is at most 13 qubits. My laptop simulated each one exactly in seconds. I checked this shortcut against the direct RX and RZZ model and against a larger 3-coupler region, and they agreed. At theta = 0.5 pi the circuit uses only Clifford gates, which a laptop can simulate for any size. So this is not a quantum advantage. A claim of quantum advantage needs a result that the best classical methods cannot match, and these shallow 3-step circuits do not come close. The run still shows how a quantum computer runs a magnet model, and that is the principle here.
